title: How the Granth is built
hookLine: 1430 pages, each called an ang, a limb: the daily banis first, then thirty-one ragas, then saloks and verses

lines: A CANOPY, A WHISK, A CLOTH.
NOT A BOOK ABOUT THE GURU.
cards: In the gurdwara, the Guru Granth Sahib rests on a raised seat under a canopy. It's wrapped in cloth, and someone waves a whisk over it, the way attendants once did for royalty.

At night, where there's a room for it, it's carried there to rest, and in the morning it's brought out again. People bow to it when they enter. To someone new, this can look like a lot of fuss over a book.
But Sikhs don't treat it as a book about the Guru. They treat it as the Guru. And that changes even the word for its pages.

teach.h: ANG — A LIMB, NOT A PAGE.
teach.b: In English you'd say page. Sikhs say ang: a limb, a part of a body. If the Granth is the living Guru, its pages aren't sheets of paper.
They're limbs. The standard edition used around the world has 1430 angs, so a hymn anywhere can be found by the same number: say ang 1, and everyone who opens the Granth lands on the same place.
It's built in three great sections, like a house with three floors.

First, the daily banis, the hymns recited every day. Ang 1 begins with the Mool Mantar and the Japji you just finished, and the opening section ends on ang 13, with the evening hymns many Sikhs recite before sleep.
Second, the heart of it: the ragas.
From ang 14, with Sri Rag, the hymns are arranged by musical mode, thirty-one ragas in all, each with its own mood and time of day. Kirtan singers still follow them.
Inside each raga, the Gurus' hymns come first, then the voices of the Bhagats. This section runs well past ang 1350.
Third, saloks and verses of many kinds, gathered at the end. On ang 1429 comes the Mundavani, the seal, with its picture of a plate holding three things: truth, contentment and reflection.
And on ang 1430, the last limb, a list of ragas.

how: In the gurdwara, the Guru Granth Sahib rests on a raised seat under a canopy, wrapped in cloth, with a chaur waved over it; Sikhs cite hymns by ang number, which is the same in every standard copy.

p: a limb: each page of the Granth

s: ang is simply the Punjabi word for page
ang means a limb; the Granth is the Guru, so its pages are limbs.

games.q: you open the Granth at ang 14. what are you looking at?
o: the start of the raga section, with Sri Rag.
games.why: angs 1 to 13 are the daily banis; from ang 14 the hymns are arranged by raga, starting with Sri Rag.

practice: Rest one hand gently on your other arm and feel it: a limb, alive, part of you, not a tool you own.

Now picture a great book open on a raised seat, each of its pages held with that same care, from ang 1, where the Mool Mantar begins, to ang 1430, where it ends. Let your hand rest there, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Ang. A limb: the word Sikhs use for each page of the Guru Granth Sahib, 1430 of them, because the Granth is the living Guru.
